Eggs of the Atlantic mackerel Scomber scombrus, when incubated at a constant temperature of 11.1 °C [T = 11.1 °C], undergo eclosion after nearly 10 days  of development. Following chorion rupture, the newly emerged yolk-sac larva, still entirely endotrophic and dependent upon its endogenous yolk reserves, measures a mere 0.37 centimeters  in total length. This lecithotrophic phase is brief but critical, as the larva must initiate the transition to exogenous feeding before its yolk reserves are fully absorbed. The interval between hatching and the moment the larva becomes fully reliant on external prey resources, effectively the time since hatch at birth, is documented as 4 days  under these same thermal conditions at a temperature of 11.1 °C [T = 11.1 °C]. The 4 day window for the trophic switch from yolk dependency to active feeding onset represents a vulnerable period wherein high mortality is frequently observed if suitable planktonic prey is unavailable. The larval total length at the point of birth, when the chorion is first ruptured, has been reported as 0.471 centimeters [Lb = 0.471 centimeters] in some studies, though this value can vary with incubation temperature as noted by MendAlva in 2007.

During the early larval phase, the exogenously feeding, free-swimming larva grows rapidly as an ichthyoplanktonic organism. Achieving a wet weight at birth of just 0.000055 grams [Wwb = 0.000055 grams], these minute teleost larvae face immense predation pressure and are highly dependent on encountering suitable densities of copepod nauplii for their first prey capture. The wet weight at this initial stage is extraordinarily low, reflecting the minuscule size of the yolk reserves allocated to each individual egg. Growth during the planktonic larval phase is characterized by allometric shifts in body proportions as the finfish larva progresses through prefixed, flexion, and postflexion stages. Eventually, the larva undergoes larval metamorphosis, a period of morphological transformation and body plan reorganisation that leads to the larval-juvenile transition. A substantial increase in body mass accompanies this developmental progression, culminating in the juvenile stage where the fish begins to more closely resemble the adult form. The ultimate wet weight that a fully grown, sexually mature adult Scomber scombrus can attain has been recorded as 2800 grams [Wwi = 2800 grams], although the average adult mass is often considerably lower depending on feeding conditions and stock density.

Reproductive maturation in the Atlantic mackerel involves a carefully timed sequence of gonadal development. The total length at puberty, which marks the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males, has been measured at 28.6 centimeters [Lp = 28.6 centimeters]. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, when individuals first initiate gamete production, is approximately 175 grams [Wwp = approximately 175 grams]. This body mass and length threshold must be attained before the hormonal cascade of the HPG axis is fully activated, leading to gonadal recrudescence and the production of viable gametes. The age at which this first reproduction event occurs has been estimated through maturity ogive data to be 2 years after hatching [tR = 2 years after hatching] when the population experiences a mean annual water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This value, however, indicates that at age 2 nearly 58% of the population is capable of spawning, showing that not all individuals mature synchronously. The process of reaching reproductive maturity involves a substantial allocation of resources to gonad development, a strategy common among iteroparous pelagic spawners that spawn multiple times across their lifespan.

The reproductive output of a spawning adult mackerel is considerable, reflecting the species high fecundity and pelagic spawning strategy. When water temperatures average 10 °C [T = 10 °C], a single large, gravid female can produce an extraordinary number of eggs over the course of a spawning season, with the maximum reproductive rate reaching approximately 10,950 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 10,950 eggs per day]. This high daily spawning output is a remarkable life-history trait for a teleost of this body size and is likely an adaptation to high larval mortality rates in the planktonic environment. The relationship between body mass and fecundity has been established through linear regression analysis, though some researchers, such as Jansen, suggest that the actual reproductive output may be lower than these regression-based estimates for the heaviest specimens. The annual reproductive effort represents a substantial energetic investment for this iteroparous species.

Field records and mark-recapture studies have provided valuable insights into the natural longevity of Scomber scombrus. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species, determined through otolith analysis of the oldest documented individuals in populations inhabiting waters with a mean annual temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], is approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years]. This considerable lifespan for a pelagic teleost allows for multiple reproductive seasons and contributes to population resilience against years of poor recruitment. In the context of its life history, the ultimate total length that an individual mackerel can achieve under favorable growth conditions has been measured at 63 centimeters [Li = 63 centimeters]. Reaching this asymptotic size involves years of sustained growth, with the fish passing through various ontogenetic niches from a pelagic larva to a piscivorous adult. The interplay between somatic growth and reproductive investment shapes the species life-history trajectory, with older individuals contributing disproportionately to the spawning stock biomass. The senescent adult death that eventually occurs marks the completion of a life cycle that can span two decades in the cooler waters of its North Atlantic range.
